Module 04 › Chapter 4.3 › Linux Firewall Management
Linux Firewall Management with nftables / firewalld
Packet filtering fundamentals, zone management, nftables examples, and safe practices for remote servers.
In this lesson

Understand how packet filtering works at the kernel level, manage firewalld zones and services, write basic nftables rules, and avoid common misconfigurations that lock out administrators.

A misconfigured firewall either leaves your server exposed or blocks critical access. These skills keep services reachable while reducing attack surface.

screens.title: What is a Firewall and Packet Filtering?
screens.narratorSegment: A firewall is a network security system that monitors and controls incoming and outgoing traffic based on predefined rules. In Linux the decision to accept, deny, or drop a packet happens in the kernel and is known as packet filtering. Packet filtering evaluates attributes such as source and destination IP, transport protocol, and destination port. This matters because services that listen on a host become reachable only when matching allow rules exist. A concrete example: if a server listens on port 22 for SSH, the firewall must permit TCP traffic to that port from the administrator's source, or remote access fails. A common misconception is that a firewall only blocks traffic from outside; in reality it governs both incoming and outgoing packets and can apply different rules per interface or zone. Key takeaway: think of packet filtering as a checklist applied to each packet. If any rule accepts it early, the packet passes; if no rule accepts it and a drop policy applies, the packet is blocked. To test understanding, ask yourself: which packet attributes would you use to limit access to a single subnet while keeping services available to trusted hosts?

content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.3 › Firewall & Packet Filtering
Core definition

A firewall enforces packet filtering rules in the kernel. Rules examine attributes like source, destination, port, and protocol to decide accept or drop.

Explainer
  • Packet attributes guide decisions: IP addresses, ports, and protocol.
  • Rules are evaluated in order; an earlier accept prevents later drops from applying.
  • Both incoming and outgoing traffic can be filtered; consider interface and source context.
Key Takeaway

Packet filtering is deterministic: rules plus policy determine whether a packet reaches a service.

Concrete example

If SSH is blocked by a drop policy, you cannot connect even if the SSH daemon is running. Allowing only your admin subnet makes access specific and reduces exposure to the internet at large.

Common mistake

Assuming the firewall is the only control. Services themselves may restrict access, and routing or NAT can change packet attributes; inspect the full path when troubleshooting.

Check your understanding

Name two packet attributes you would include in a rule to limit SSH to a specific host and why each matters.

screens.title: firewalld Overview and Zone Model
screens.narratorSegment: firewalld is a dynamic firewall manager often used on Red Hat-based systems. Its central idea is the zone: a named set of rules representing a trust level for network interfaces or sources. Common zones include public for untrusted networks and internal or home for trusted networks. Using zones means you can assign an interface or source to a trust level and rely on the zone's services and ports. For example, a server connected to an internal network can use the internal zone to allow additional services that would be unsafe on the public zone. A common misstep is treating zones like single-use profiles; in reality you can bind zones to interfaces, IP addresses, or rich rules for fine-grained control. An example workflow is to list active zones, inspect the public zone configuration, add SSH permanently to the public zone, reload firewalld, and verify. The core idea is to organize permissions by trust so that the same service allowance does not need repeated low-level rules. Consider this approach a policy layer on top of packet-filtering tables. firewalld Overview and Zone Model means zones group rules by trust level. assign network interfaces or sources to zones to apply consistent sets of allowed services and ports.. In practical terms, zones, trust levels, and how they simplify firewall management. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 04 › Chapter 4.3 › firewalld Zones
Zone architecture
Zones

Zones are named profiles that contain allowed services, ports, and rules. Interfaces and source addresses are assigned to a zone to apply its policies.

Typical zones
  • public: untrusted networks
  • internal / home: trusted local networks
Commands to inspect
sudo firewall-cmd --get-active-zones
sudo firewall-cmd --list-all --zone=public
Example

Allow SSH and HTTP in the public zone permanently, then reload to apply the permanent configuration.

sudo firewall-cmd --zone=public --add-service=ssh --permanent
sudo firewall-cmd --zone=public --add-service=http --permanent
sudo firewall-cmd --reload
Misconception

Adding a service at runtime without --permanent creates a temporary rule that disappears after reboot or service restart. Always remember to persist important rules.

Module 04 › Chapter 4.3 › firewall-cmd Workflow
Command walkthrough
sudo systemctl enable firewalld --now
sudo firewall-cmd --state
sudo firewall-cmd --get-active-zones
sudo firewall-cmd --list-all --zone=public
sudo firewall-cmd --zone=public --add-service=ssh --permanent
sudo firewall-cmd --zone=public --add-service=http --permanent
sudo firewall-cmd --zone=public --add-port=8080/tcp --permanent
sudo firewall-cmd --reload
sudo firewall-cmd --list-all --zone=public
Checklist
  • Use predefined services when available for clarity.
  • Use --permanent to persist rules across reboots.
  • Reload firewalld to apply permanent rules immediately.
Common mistake

Adding a port or service without --permanent is temporary. If you reboot or restart firewalld, the change will disappear unless persisted.

Pro tip

Open SSH first and test from a separate connection before making broader changes. Keep a console or recovery method ready.

screens.title: nftables: Tables, Chains, and Policies
screens.narratorSegment: nftables is the modern Linux packet-filtering framework that replaces iptables and provides a unified syntax for IPv4, IPv6, bridging, and NAT. Its basic building blocks are tables, chains, and rules. A table contains chains; a chain is a list of rules that the kernel evaluates for matching packets. Chains can be attached to hooks such as input, forward, or output and have a default policy, like accept or drop. Setting a policy drop on an input chain means that packets not explicitly accepted will be blocked. A concrete example from the chapter shows creating a table named filter and an input chain with policy drop, then adding rules to accept loopback traffic, established connections, SSH, and a local subnet. A common misunderstanding is that rules are unordered; in nftables the sequential order matters because the first matching rule determines the outcome. Key takeaway: design an explicit allow list with a safe order—established and loopback first, then administrative services—to prevent accidental lockout. nftables: Tables, Chains, and Policies means tables group chains; chains have ordered rules and a default policy. order and explicit accepts with a drop policy create a safe allow-list architecture.. In practical terms, how nftables structures rules and the default policy concept. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.3 › nftables Structure
Concepts
  • Table: container for chains, often named by address family like ip or ip6.
  • Chain: ordered list of rules associated with a hook and a default policy.
  • Rule: single conditional that accepts or drops matching packets.
Important pattern

Place loopback and established/related accept rules before service accepts, then set a default drop policy to create a minimal and safe allow list.

Example commands
sudo nft add table ip filter
sudo nft add chain ip filter input { type filter hook input priority 0 ; policy drop ; }
sudo nft add rule ip filter input iif "lo" accept
sudo nft add rule ip filter input ct state established,related accept
sudo nft add rule ip filter input tcp dport ssh accept
sudo nft add rule ip filter input ip saddr 192.168.1.0/24 accept
Misconception

Assuming rules are unordered. In nftables the order matters; ensure accepts for essentials come before any broad drops.

screens.title: nftables Example Ruleset Explained
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through a minimal nftables example step by step so you understand why each line exists. First, creating the table establishes the container: add table ip filter. Next we add an input chain attached to the input hook with type filter and a priority; importantly we set policy drop so that anything not explicitly accepted is blocked. Then add a rule to accept loopback traffic by matching the loopback interface. This rule is necessary for inter-process communication that relies on localhost. The next rule accepts established and related connections—this prevents breaking return traffic for connections you initiated. After that we permit TCP destination port SSH so administrators can connect. Another rule can allow a local subnet by matching source address. Each rule is deliberate: loopback and established first, service accepts next, then source-specific allowances. A common error is applying the drop policy before these accepts or not testing from another client. The takeaway: order rules to protect access while enforcing a deny-by-default posture. nftables Example Ruleset Explained means loopback and established accepts must come before service accepts and the default drop policy to keep services functional and avoid lockout.. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.3 › nftables Example
Ruleset (annotated)
# Create table
sudo nft add table ip filter

# Create input chain with drop policy
sudo nft add chain ip filter input { type filter hook input priority 0 ; policy drop ; }

# Accept loopback
sudo nft add rule ip filter input iif "lo" accept

# Accept established and related
sudo nft add rule ip filter input ct state established,related accept

# Accept SSH
sudo nft add rule ip filter input tcp dport ssh accept

# Allow local subnet
sudo nft add rule ip filter input ip saddr 192.168.1.0/24 accept
Explanation cards
Loopback
Essential for local services. Accept it to avoid breaking system behavior.
Established
Allows return traffic for connections you initiated, preventing accidental breaks.
Service accepts
Add only the services you need, such as SSH and HTTP, to reduce exposure.
Key Takeaway

Order your rules: loopback, established, then service and source accepts, with a final drop policy to deny anything else.

screens.narratorSegment: nftables configuration is commonly stored in /etc/nftables. conf and loaded at boot, which ensures your rules persist across reboots. A minimal configuration begins with a flush ruleset line to clear existing rules, then defines the table, chains, and rules. After saving the file, apply it with sudo nft -f /etc/nftables. conf to test it immediately. Verification is critical: use sudo nft list ruleset to inspect the active ruleset and confirm that your table, chain, and rules exist and are in the expected order. A practical example in the chapter shows a configuration that flushes, creates a filter table, defines an input chain with policy drop, and adds rules for loopback, established/related, SSH, HTTP, and a custom port 8080. A common trap is forgetting to ensure you have console or alternate access before applying a drop policy; always validate with a temporary rule or remote test. Key takeaway: save, apply, and then verify the ruleset output to confirm the firewall behaves as expected. content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.3 › Persisting nftables
Example /etc/nftables.conf
#!/usr/sbin/nft -f

flush ruleset

table ip filter {
    chain input {
        type filter hook input priority 0; policy drop;

        # accept established and related connections
        ct state established,related accept

        # accept traffic on loopback interface
        iif "lo" accept

        # accept SSH connections
        tcp dport 22 accept

        # accept HTTP connections
        tcp dport 80 accept

        # accept custom port 8080
        tcp dport 8080 accept
    }
}
Apply and verify
sudo nft -f /etc/nftables.conf
sudo nft list ruleset
Safety note

Before applying a drop policy, ensure alternate access exists or add a temporary rule to avoid locking yourself out.

Key Takeaway

Save rules to /etc/nftables.conf, apply with nft -f, and always confirm the rule order using nft list ruleset.

screens.title: Avoiding Lockout: Administrative Access and Safety Rules
screens.narratorSegment: A critical safety concern when changing firewall rules on a remote server is locking yourself out. Before applying restrictive rules or a drop policy, ensure you have at least one persistent allowance for administrative access or an alternate recovery path. Concrete safeguards include permitting your admin IP address or range explicitly, keeping a temporary open SSH rule while testing, or ensuring console or physical access is available. Another practical approach is to apply rules in a scripted or timed manner: make a change and, if it fails, automatically revert after a short window. The chapter emphasizes keeping established and related accepts in your ruleset so return traffic for existing sessions continues. A common misconception is that adding a single SSH accept is always sufficient—if your source IP is dynamic, you may need to allow a broader range or rely on VPN-based management. Key takeaway: plan recovery first, test from a separate host, and persist rules only after verification to prevent accidental lockout. fullNarratorScript:
Firewalls act as gatekeepers on Linux systems, controlling which packets are allowed, denied, or dropped. In this chapter you will learn what packet filtering means at the kernel level, how higher-level tools like firewalld make rules easier to manage on Red Hat systems, and how nftables structures rules into tables and chains. We'll walk through common firewall-cmd commands to list zones, add services and ports, and make rules permanent, and we'll examine a practical nftables example that sets a default drop policy while allowing loopback, established connections, SSH and HTTP. You will also learn safety practices to avoid locking yourself out of a remote server and common misconfigurations to watch for. By the end you will be able to inspect an active ruleset, add a service or port safely, persist changes, and craft a minimal nftables ruleset. Think of this chapter as a set of practical, repeatable steps to make a Linux host network-safe without losing access.

In this chapter you will learn four practical competencies that map directly to real administrative tasks. First, you will understand packet filtering: what it means for the kernel to inspect packets and the criteria used to accept or drop them. This matters because every service that listens on a server is exposed unless filtered, and understanding packet filtering helps you make targeted rules. Second, you will be able to configure and manage firewalld zones, services, and ports on Red Hat-based systems. That includes listing active zones and adding services or ports permanently. A concrete example is enabling SSH and HTTP in the public zone and reloading to apply changes. Third, you will implement basic nftables rules: creating a table and input chain, setting a default drop policy, and adding rules for loopback, established connections, SSH and a custom port. Practically, this means writing a small /etc/nftables. conf and applying it. Fourth, you will identify common misconfigurations and apply best practices—such as testing rules, persisting configuration, and avoiding overly permissive rules that use any-source addresses. Each objective includes a small practical test you can try on a lab VM to confirm competency.

These practical tasks translate objectives into lab steps so you can demonstrate competence. Start by enabling and checking firewalld: enable the service and confirm state. Then list active zones and inspect a zone, which helps you verify what traffic is allowed by default. Next, add a service like SSH or HTTP to the public zone permanently and then reload firewalld so the rule persists; test from another machine to confirm connectivity. For nftables, write a short configuration file that flushes the ruleset, creates an ip filter table, and defines an input chain with a policy drop while explicitly allowing loopback, established connections, SSH and HTTP. Apply the nftables configuration and verify the ruleset output. Finally, run a checklist: ensure changes are saved, avoid opening 0.0.0.0/0 unnecessarily, confirm SSH remains reachable, and document your rules. Each task reinforces the practical skill of making and validating firewall changes safely.

A firewall is a network security system that monitors and controls incoming and outgoing traffic based on predefined rules. In Linux the decision to accept, deny, or drop a packet happens in the kernel and is known as packet filtering. Packet filtering evaluates attributes such as source and destination IP, transport protocol, and destination port. This matters because services that listen on a host become reachable only when matching allow rules exist. A concrete example: if a server listens on port 22 for SSH, the firewall must permit TCP traffic to that port from the administrator's source, or remote access fails. A common misconception is that a firewall only blocks traffic from outside; in reality it governs both incoming and outgoing packets and can apply different rules per interface or zone. Key takeaway: think of packet filtering as a checklist applied to each packet. If any rule accepts it early, the packet passes; if no rule accepts it and a drop policy applies, the packet is blocked. To test understanding, ask yourself: which packet attributes would you use to limit access to a single subnet while keeping services available to trusted hosts?

firewalld is a dynamic firewall manager often used on Red Hat-based systems. Its central idea is the zone: a named set of rules representing a trust level for network interfaces or sources. Common zones include public for untrusted networks and internal or home for trusted networks. Using zones means you can assign an interface or source to a trust level and rely on the zone's services and ports. For example, a server connected to an internal network can use the internal zone to allow additional services that would be unsafe on the public zone. A common misstep is treating zones like single-use profiles; in reality you can bind zones to interfaces, IP addresses, or rich rules for fine-grained control. An example workflow is to list active zones, inspect the public zone configuration, add SSH permanently to the public zone, reload firewalld, and verify. The core idea is to organize permissions by trust so that the same service allowance does not need repeated low-level rules. Consider this approach a policy layer on top of packet-filtering tables. firewalld Overview and Zone Model means zones group rules by trust level. assign network interfaces or sources to zones to apply consistent sets of allowed services and ports.. In practical terms, zones, trust levels, and how they simplify firewall management. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Working with firewalld follows a repeatable, safe workflow: check state, list active zones, add rules, persist them, reload, and verify. First, enable and confirm the service, which ensures the dynamic manager runs and applies your changes. Listing active zones and inspecting the public zone reveals current services and ports. When opening access for a service, prefer the predefined service name where available; it is descriptive and maps to the correct ports and protocols. Use the --permanent flag when you want rules to survive reboots, and follow with a reload so they take effect immediately. A concrete example sequence is enabling firewalld, adding SSH and HTTP permanently, and reloading. A common mistake is adding runtime rules without --permanent, which vanish after a reboot. Another trap is forgetting to test access from a separate client before closing your current session; always validate SSH with a second connection or console access ready. Key takeaway: follow enable → list → add with --permanent → reload → verify to apply safe, persistent rules. firewalld Commands: Listing, Adding, and Persisting means enable service, list zones, add services or ports with --permanent, reload to apply, and verify access from another host.. In practical terms, common firewall-cmd commands and a safe workflow. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

nftables is the modern Linux packet-filtering framework that replaces iptables and provides a unified syntax for IPv4, IPv6, bridging, and NAT. Its basic building blocks are tables, chains, and rules. A table contains chains; a chain is a list of rules that the kernel evaluates for matching packets. Chains can be attached to hooks such as input, forward, or output and have a default policy, like accept or drop. Setting a policy drop on an input chain means that packets not explicitly accepted will be blocked. A concrete example from the chapter shows creating a table named filter and an input chain with policy drop, then adding rules to accept loopback traffic, established connections, SSH, and a local subnet. A common misunderstanding is that rules are unordered; in nftables the sequential order matters because the first matching rule determines the outcome. Key takeaway: design an explicit allow list with a safe order—established and loopback first, then administrative services—to prevent accidental lockout. nftables: Tables, Chains, and Policies means tables group chains; chains have ordered rules and a default policy. order and explicit accepts with a drop policy create a safe allow-list architecture.. In practical terms, how nftables structures rules and the default policy concept. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Let's walk through a minimal nftables example step by step so you understand why each line exists. First, creating the table establishes the container: add table ip filter. Next we add an input chain attached to the input hook with type filter and a priority; importantly we set policy drop so that anything not explicitly accepted is blocked. Then add a rule to accept loopback traffic by matching the loopback interface. This rule is necessary for inter-process communication that relies on localhost. The next rule accepts established and related connections—this prevents breaking return traffic for connections you initiated. After that we permit TCP destination port SSH so administrators can connect. Another rule can allow a local subnet by matching source address.
